title.undergrad: How MRI contrast works: T1 and T2

summary.undergrad: The same head, scanned two ways. On the [[t1|T1]] image in pane A, fluid is dark and [[white-matter|white matter]] is bright. On the [[t2|T2]] image in pane B, fluid is bright. Pane A is the main view and pane B the second one; the cursor is linked, so both always show the same spot.
summary.med: Compare CSF, white matter and vitreous on a 3D T1 MPRAGE (A) and an axial T2 turbo spin echo (B). T1 weighting reflects longitudinal relaxation: fat and myelinated white matter have short T1 and look bright. T2 weighting reflects transverse relaxation: free water has a long T2 and looks bright. Pane A is the main view and pane B the second one; the cursor is linked, so both always show the same spot.

text.undergrad: Dark on T1, bright on T2. A quick rule: on T2, water is white.
text.med: CSF: long T1 and long T2, so hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2.

text.undergrad: Bright on T1 and darker grey on T2. Its fatty myelin insulation is what makes it bright on T1.
text.med: Myelinated white matter: shorter T1 and T2 than grey matter, so brighter than cortex on T1 and darker than cortex on T2.

text.undergrad: The fluid-filled eye behaves like the ventricles: dark on T1, bright on T2.
text.med: Vitreous humour is mostly free water: hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, like CSF.
